transcript.text: Hi, our integrated fridge freezer (behind a kitchen door) - the fridge is around 10 degrees but the freezer seems ok. We had a power cut a week ago, not sure if related. Rented flat, can't really take it out.

A fridge at around 10°C while the freezer still seems fine usually means the cooling is working but isn't getting into the fridge properly, rather than the whole system failing. The power cut could be related, or it could be coincidence. These are the most likely causes, roughly in order: 1. A setting has changed. Some electronic models reset or drop into a holiday or eco mode after a power cut.
2. Cold air isn't reaching the fridge. On a frost-free model, one coil behind the freezer's back panel cools both sections. If vents are blocked, or ice has built up on that coil because of a defrost problem, the freezer stays cold and the fridge goes warm. On a non-frost-free model, a thick ice build-up on the fridge back wall or a blocked drain hole can do the same thing.
3. Less likely, the small internal fan has stopped, or a door seal isn't closing properly. These checks are all safe and don't need the unit taken out: 1. Settings: check the dial or display. The fridge should be about 3–5°C and the freezer -18°C, with no holiday or eco mode on. If something was wrong, correct it and give it 24 hours.
2. Vents and loading: if there are vents on the fridge's back wall, make sure nothing is pressed against them. If a vent was blocked, that may be the whole problem.
3. Back wall and drain: look for a sheet of ice or pooled water on the fridge back wall, and check the little drain hole near the bottom. You can clear it gently with warm water from a squeezy bottle, but don't use anything sharp. Ice or water there points to a drain or defrost issue.
4. The fan: with the freezer door open, press the door-light switch in by hand and listen. A whirr means the fan has power, so a hidden ice blockage becomes more likely. Silence on a frost-free model points towards the fan.
5. Door seals and vents: run your fingers round both door seals for gaps or folds. Also check the vent grille in the plinth below the door isn't blocked or dusty. Integrated units need that airflow. It also helps to get a real temperature reading. Put a thermometer in a glass of water on a middle shelf and leave it overnight. A 'freezer seems ok' feeling isn't always accurate. If nothing obvious turns up, the next step for a suspected ice blockage is a full defrost. That means switching off and leaving it for most of a day with towels down, then seeing if it recovers. Thanks. The dial inside is on 3 out of 5, and there's no display. My thermometer says 10C in the fridge and -16C in the freezer. I can't see any vent in the fridge, and the plinth grille looks clear. The fridge door closes, but the cabinet door moves with it. I haven't checked the fridge back wall or the drain hole, and I'm not sure how to check the fan. No burning smell and nothing tripping, but I can hear it running a lot.

On the fan: you may not have one. A dial with no display and no vents inside the fridge usually means the fridge is 'static', which is common in integrated models. It has its own cold plate hidden behind the back wall and no fan. Here's how to tell, and how to listen for a fan if there is one: 1. Does the freezer frost up? If you get frost on the drawers or walls and have to defrost it now and then, it isn't frost-free, so there's no fan to check. If it never frosts and has a panel with slots at the back of the freezer, it's probably frost-free with a fan.
2. If it does seem frost-free, open the freezer door. Find the little button the door presses (usually on the frame) and hold it in by hand. Listen for a soft whirr from behind the back panel. Some fans only run while the motor is running, so try it when you can hear it humming. Silence then points to the fan. A whirr means the fan is fine. Based on what you've found, the likely causes for a static fridge are: 1. Ice or water on the fridge back wall. Switch it off at the socket, open the fridge and look at the back wall. A thick sheet of ice, or water pooling because the drain hole near the bottom is blocked, stops it cooling. Clear the hole gently with warm water from a squeezy bottle. Heavy ice needs a full defrost: switch off for most of a day with towels down and the freezer food kept cold elsewhere.
2. The back wall never gets properly cold. Check it after the fridge has been running a while. A healthy wall feels very cold and usually has a light frost or droplets that come and go. If it stays barely cool even though it's running a lot, that points to a problem in the sealed cooling system. The freezer at -16°C is a little warmer than ideal, which fits that. That's an engineer job.
3. The door. Integrated fridges hang the kitchen door on slides, so it moving with the fridge door is normal. If the kitchen door is out of line, though, it can stop the fridge door pressing fully shut. Close it on a strip of paper at several points round the seal. If the paper pulls out easily anywhere, warm air is getting in. As it's a rented flat, let your landlord know now. If it turns out to be the cooling system or needs the unit pulling out, that's for their engineer to deal with. Meanwhile, keep the fridge at 10°C in mind for food safety. Move milk, meat and leftovers to the freezer or a cool box.
The freezer does have some frost on the back wall, but not loads. Is that enough to tell if it's frost-free? I haven't looked at the fridge back wall or the drain hole yet.

Yes, that's a good enough clue. Frost-free freezers keep their cooling coil hidden behind a panel and clear it automatically, so you normally see little or no frost on the walls. In that kind of fridge, the cooling comes from a cold plate hidden behind the fridge's back wall. 1. Ice or water problems on that back wall. A thick ice sheet, or water that can't drain away, stops the plate cooling the fridge properly. This is the hopeful one, because a defrost and clearing the drain can sort it.
2. The plate isn't getting properly cold. If it's running a lot but the back wall stays only cool, that points to a sealed cooling system fault such as lost refrigerant. That's an engineer job. The freezer being a couple of degrees warmer than ideal fits this. 1. When you've heard it running for a while, open the fridge and look at the back wall. Then touch it.
2. A thick sheet of ice, or water pooling at the bottom, points to cause 1. Clear the drain hole gently with warm water as described before. If there's heavy ice, do a full defrost (off at the socket, towels down, food kept cold elsewhere).
3. If it feels very cold, with light frost or droplets that come and go, the plate is working. Then the door is the next suspect. Try the paper-strip test round the seal.
4. If it feels barely cool despite all that running, that points to the sealed system. Pass it to your landlord for an engineer. Meanwhile, keep perishables in the freezer or a cool box, since 10°C isn't safe for milk, meat or leftovers.
Ok, I'll have a look at the fridge back wall once it's been running a bit. Just to check, if it turns out to be the sealed system, I just report it to the letting agent, right?

Yes, that's right. In a rented flat the fridge freezer is usually the landlord's appliance, so a sealed system fault is theirs to arrange and pay for. It's also not something you should attempt, as it needs a refrigeration engineer. Report it to the letting agent in writing (email is fine) so there's a record. 1. The fridge is at 10°C on a thermometer and the freezer at -16°C, with the dial on 3.
2. It runs a lot.
3. 4. 5. It's an integrated unit, so it may need pulling out. The main exception is if the fridge is yours rather than part of the letting, or your tenancy says otherwise. Worth a quick look if you're unsure. You can report it now rather than waiting. A fridge at 10°C is a food-safety problem whichever cause it turns out to be, and agents can be slow to book someone. 1. Thick ice or pooled water: probably the drain or an ice build-up, which you may be able to sort with a defrost and by clearing the drain hole. Tell the agent if you do this and whether it worked.
2. The door seal or kitchen door alignment then becomes the main suspect.
3. Barely cool even after a long run: this points to the sealed system. Add that to your report so the engineer knows what to expect.
